captions.text: Recap of chapter 31: planted text sent a payroll code out in 18 runs of 40.
A warning in the prompt didn't help. The attack lives in the prompt too.
Limits in code held, however the model was talked into it.
And the Rule of Two: give an agent at most two of three risky abilities.
Today's black box: switching models. Chapter 13 made it one line. Today we use that line.
Switching takes one line. Knowing it worked takes the eval.
One question through chapter 30's agent, on the 7B model you've used all course. It's right.
Now one line changes: a model twice the size. Predict: better, or worse?
It wrote 84 tokens, and the agent got nothing back. Three empty replies, then an error.
The full eval: 42 questions, three times each. 113 out of 126 became 14. Nothing crashed.
77 answers came back partly in Thai or Chinese, to an English question.
What did each model really write? The 7B model writes one tool call, and stops.
The 14B model writes the same call, then keeps going, and answers from a search it imagined.
$50 from cash_management.md. Neither exists. And Ollama can't parse it, so it returns nothing.
One sentence in the prompt: write only the tool call, then stop. On this question, it works.
On the eval it reached 33 of 126. A fix for one model has to be tested again on the next.
So, a cloud model. It needs a key, kept in .env, which git ignores. Never in code, never on screen.
This key is fake. Google's real reply: not valid. A 400 won't fix itself, so don't retry.
GeminiModel translates our messages by hand. The system prompt goes apart, and roles are user and model.
A tool result goes back as a user turn, matched to its call by id.
Gemini also sends a thought signature, which must go back exactly as received.
So Message gets one field only the provider reads. The framework carries it without opening it.
Options don't travel. num_ctx exists only in Ollama, and newer Gemini models ignore temperature.
So GeminiModel refuses any option it doesn't know, instead of dropping it quietly.
A cloud model charges per token. SpendLimit refuses the next call once the limit is reached.
It adds up each reply's cost, thinking included. All our cloud runs together cost $0.57.
The switch: the same agent, tool and index. Only the model string changed. Right, for $0.0002.
On one pass of the eval, Flash-Lite got 41 of 42, for about two cents.
3.6 Flash got 36. It kept searching until our step limit stopped it, a limit chosen for 7B.
Chapter 30's 40 long tools: both local models choke on Ollama's window. Both cloud models got every one.
One tiny reply, three times on each model. The cloud models took about 2 seconds.
The newest Flash model took over two minutes to say ok. Speed changes, so you measure it.
The agent, tools and eval ran unchanged on four models. But the message format had to grow.
Options didn't travel. An option one provider ignores is a bug you can't see.
Behaviour didn't travel: one model wrote past its call, one hit the step limit, one was too slow.
And the cloud brought a key, a spending limit and new errors.
Five exercises: a Gemini part, a reply's cost, options, a .env line and a budget. No key needed.
You've finished when you see 5 passed.
